chapters.html:
Valorous death before glorious return.

One simple phrase, a conviction every Kremnoan shares. Bearing the title of the Crown Prince, it has been seared into Mydei’s very core.

A warrior’s death is a subject of reverence for Kremnoans, rivaling those who follow the Death Titan with utmost devotion. It’s almost logical, seeing as Strife and Death are but two sides of the same coin. Two-thirds of the Titans of Calamity.

For all their worship, Kremnoans rarely contemplate the consequences of one’s demise.

Grief has always been looked down upon, as all who have fallen in battle are awaited by the places of honor reserved for them in the afterlife. In the army, Mydei has witnessed many family members smiling through their tears at the memorials hosted for their deceased relatives during the desertion from Castrum Kremnos, careful not to show the sorrow they experienced lest it be viewed as disrespect.

What does it matter what happens after, when you have already achieved the greatest honor you could dream of?

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

But what does one see when their body ceases all its functions?

It’s a question he should have known the answer to before anything else. Death and the horizon stretching with freezing water raise him through almost a decade of his life, one agonizing moment at a time. By irony’s fate, there are no memories of the past stored in his brain to recall upon the moment of death, only the vicious cycle repeating itself day in and day out. Lungs forever twisting with the burning sensation, water spilling through his lips each time he gasps back into life.

The blinding light shining through the water’s surface as he yet again drowns in its depths is the first thing out of the ordinary that he has witnessed in however many years. He reaches out to it with his hand, foolishly attempting to clutch at it. Once he resurfaces and coughs mouthfuls of water out, he sees the bright star in the dark sky, unmoving, as if it has been waiting for something.

It takes only a few more days for the Sea of Souls to spit him out of its clutches, suddenly done with its unyielding torture. He props himself up weakly, still half-submerged in the water as he observes the star and, for the first time in his life, gains a sense of purpose.

A wish for something other than, ‘Please, let it end.’

He crawls through the blackened shores and teaches himself to walk on the legs he had never used on land before. It is shaky and he stumbles on every step, falling onto the ground and cutting himself on sharp stones until he leaves a trail of golden blood in his wake. Fortunately, the movement isn’t too dissimilar from treading through the water. It’s the first skill he learned on his own, instinctually, when his body gained enough muscle and strength to do anything other than flail.

Slowly, he makes his way through the land, following the star until he discovers something that resembles civilization. A concerned woman finds him in the fields, fretting over the frostbitten limbs and malnourishment in words he cannot understand just yet. He watches her curiously as she drapes a red coat over him, carrying his small figure back to the village where people eventually help him out.

It takes a while to learn a language for the first time. Despite the adults helping him as much as they can and teaching him the necessary skills to take care of himself on his own, he never develops a feeling of belonging or affection for the village. In the future, he might be grateful for them, but he won’t remember their names or the location of the settlement. Just an outsider, kept in stasis until he is old enough to move on from there.

Then, a warrior passes by the village about a year in.

He hears of it from other kids. She intends to stay a few days, restock the supplies, and set out to her homeland after a battle that had left her as the sole survivor. He doesn’t particularly care when they tell him, not until a day later when he is play-fighting with another kid and she sits on the bench nearby, watching them with careful consideration.

He isn’t as scrawny as he used to be when he first arrived at the village, bones no longer breaking at the slightest impact due to insufficient diet. Or lack of food in general. He found out it isn’t normal for your stomach to feel like it’s attempting to devour itself all the time rather quickly. But the boy he is fighting against is older than him, taller by a head, and holding more strength in his muscles.

He is usually able to avoid any direct punches and is quicker on his feet than other kids. This time, his opponent manages to wrestle him into place before kicking him in the stomach and sending him stumbling back.

The other kids cheer at the action, having never once taken the side of the strange foreigner.

He clicks his tongue in annoyance as he lands on the wooden fence, one of the rusted nails catching him on the forearm. He pays it no mind, used to the pain more intense than that, and instead pushes himself off the wooden structure. He uses the momentum to kick right into the boy’s knee to throw off his balance. Then, he delivers a firm punch to the jaw, putting his entire body weight into it, making him yell in pain as he stumbles a few paces back.

He startles when the woman grabs his arm out of nowhere, having never noticed her approaching them in the first place. Her grip on his wrist is painfully tight—enough to bruise—as she looks at his wound with narrowed eyes.

“You are bleeding with ichor, child,” she says. A statement rather than a question, but her gaze asks for elaboration.

He doesn’t answer, yanking his arm out of her grip. An action possible only because she allowed for it.

“He doesn’t speak much,” a boy he was fighting with tells her, spitting a few times onto the ground with red liquid before a tooth follows.

He sees some adults starting to make their way over, possibly to check what the fuss is about, as the woman’s narrowed gaze moves to his face, eyes jumping from one point to another. A man walks close enough to ask whether everything is alright, but no sound comes out of his mouth when she continues.

“You bear striking resemblance to our late Queen,” she muses, grabbing him by the chin and twisting it this and that way to take a better look. “Your eyes are a perfect replica of hers, and so are your delicate yet sharp features.”

Ignoring the stifling silence falling around them, he only feels the agitation at being handled like an unruly animal. He clutches at her forearm to keep himself steady and sinks his teeth into the flesh of her hand, a metallic taste filling his mouth.

The woman doesn’t let go as he expected. Instead, she simply laughs. Doesn’t even twitch. “Fierce cub. Befitting of the child of Gorgo,” she comments with a smirk and finally releases her hold on him, palm stained with crimson. He swipes his hand at his mouth, smearing the blood further as he stares at her in defiance. “Tell me, boy, what’s your first memory of?”

He doesn’t trust her. He wants nothing to do with the woman. And yet, he can’t help the feeling of anticipation rising from deep within at the prospect of learning something, anything, about his origin. “Sea,” he eventually responds with reluctance, much to her satisfaction.

The villagers are all too eager to let him leave with the warrior when they learn of his possible connection to the city-state called Castrum Kremnos. Afraid of what, he didn’t know at the time.

On the first night, once they are far enough, she decides to test her hypothesis. She drives a knife right into his heart and welcomes him back to life with a smile. She couldn’t have taken a stray child back without being certain about his identity, she explains. He is too confused to think much about it, beyond the vague impression of being glad it hurt less than drowning.

It is the first time he sees a vivid memory in a brief moment after death, feeling like he is living through it again. For a few minutes, he felt himself resting on a stranger’s hip as she carried him away, bundled in the warm cloth and with her hand covering the back of his head protectively. The first act of kindness he ever experienced.

It’s at ten years old that he learns his name is Mydeimos, the lost Crown Prince, and that when one’s body ceases all its functions, you relive your memories.

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

Death becomes a common currency to him, a teenager assembling a detachment army outside of the borders of his homeland. One that he hasn’t ever stepped foot in. Krateros finds him once Mydei’s soldiers start gaining renown for their achievements, separate from Castrum Kremnos, yet hailing from it. His mentor teaches him all he can, from refining Mydei’s fighting skills to the traditions no one ever told him about.

Mydei brushes death off as it refuses to take hold of him, discarding the visions as he pushes through to regain consciousness as fast as possible, to keep as many people safe as he can, to tear the throats of their enemies out before someone other than him can get hurt.

It’s only once he fulfills the goal that served as his driving force for over a decade and kills King Eurypon, taking the Kremnoan Detachment to Okhema and pledging alliance to the blonde usurper and accepting the title of the Chrysos Heir, that things slow down enough for him to parse through what he’s been through. The first nine years of his life, the first contact with the rest of humanity, the process of learning how to live, gaining people he cares about and wishes to protect only to lose them one by one, having enough pleasant experiences for them to flash in front of his eyes.

Time to ponder over the subject of death itself and his relationship with it. He finds out he enjoys the peacefulness of it, the adrenaline at meeting his own demise just to spring back up without a scratch left on his body, the process punctuated only by the brief moment of living through the best of his memories once more.

The ability to hear Peucesta’s music that accompanied them everywhere again. To watch Perdikkas scold them but still heal them to the best of his ability again. To be teased endlessly by Hephaestion, sparring with him in the dirt as others watch on with exasperation again.

It becomes preferable to the stagnancy of the agonizingly lengthy wait Aglaea put them on, deeming them not ready to move against the Titans. Easier than remembering all victims of the black tide he failed to save. The brief period of no thoughts and sweet emptiness makes it less difficult to live with himself once he finds out he is the reason for his mother’s death and his father’s spiral into madness.

It’s addicting.

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

“You are taking longer nowadays, Lord Mydei,” Castorice says quietly, a touch of concern coloring her voice. From the sound of it, she is sitting a few paces away from his bedside as he comes to.

He won't ask how long it took for him to wake up this time. It's enough that the memory felt like it lasted days, witnessing the carefree hours of traveling through cities with his friends, the Kremnoan Detachment at their backs.

Mydei releases a long sigh, scowling silently. He is too exhausted to request Castorice to drop that honorific, it’s not like she’s going to listen anyway. Too proper, too respectful. Even Phainon couldn’t get through her just yet to gain that familiarity, which means Mydei doesn’t stand a chance either.

She is also right in her assessment.

With every death added to the tally, Mydei struggles to open his eyes again just a little more. He leads a battle with himself, subconsciously clutching onto the tranquility of it, hoping against the hope it might be the last time. Guilt stabs him in the gut every time, but he can’t help it. Is it really so selfish of him to wish for rest? Hasn’t he gone through enough?

He will fight to the best of his ability as long as the curse deems him fit to uphold the prophecy, taking care of his people and standing in their defense. But it won’t stop him from childishly seeking a way to relieve the pain of his immortal existence.

Blindly, he reaches the small table at his bedside with his hand, grabbing the glass of water resting in the exact same spot on it as it always does. It’s a tradition, at this point, the movement is practiced and performed while barely awake.

He pushes himself up in the bed just slightly so he doesn’t choke, downing it in one go. He will feel sick later for not giving his stomach time to adjust.

“Perhaps I’m finally getting closer to earning the luxury of eternal sleep,” he muses drily, finally opening his eyes. Castorice watches him, hands folded neatly in her lap. “We could test that theory if you came closer.”

Castorice’s lips twist with sorrow, knuckles turning pale as her grip tightens. “Please do not joke like that,” she says mildly. “You are an important figure, Lord Mydei. We cherish your company, and I am unsure whether some of us would have been able to recover from such loss.”

Mydei snorts without any humor. It’s not that he doesn’t think he is useful. He knows his skills are vital, possibly the only chance at slaying Nikador. But it’s not like he is exceptionally close with any of them. Aglaea would have found it inconvenient. Castorice would have lost someone who understands her domain almost as intimately as she does. Phainon would have mourned the demise of a sparring partner before finding another poor sod to bother.

Maybe if he died permanently, the prophecy would have chosen another worthy soul.

“Do not fret,” he says in an attempt at reassurance. “The curse won’t release me from its hold so easily.”

Castorice doesn’t seem to be appeased by his words, brows furrowed as she studies him. She looks like she wants to say something but changes her mind, sighing softly in resignation. She stays by his side for one more hour, the death she carries with her silent and comforting to Mydei. Familiar.

Until Phainon barges in, voice soft but gaze heavy as he takes a seat on Mydei’s bed. It doesn’t even take five minutes before they’re throwing scathing remarks at one another that neither of them means, Castorice chuckling quietly into her hand.

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

Mydei isn’t a stranger to taking his own life.

The whole ordeal loses some of the significance when you willingly drown yourself in the sea as a child, hoping it might cut your misery short. Or if you are forced to bash your head into the stone—pierce your skull, slice your throat, put your own guts back in your body, tear the—to kickstart the healing factor in order to save your allies one too many times.

It usually happens out of convenience. But not always.

Plagued by the guilt and weight of the lack of control that has been plucked from his hands by fate itself, he finds a quiet spot in the ruins just outside of Okhema and sits down, his favorite dagger clutched in his hand.

It’s been a long week. Month. However long, time loses meaning at a certain point.

But it doesn’t change the fact that he feels like something is consuming him alive. It’s been too long since the last time somebody killed him, allowed the visions containing not a single negative thread of emotion to swim into the forefront of his brain, overriding everything else.

He knows it’s unbecoming of him to fall apart so easily. Would anyone still want to follow him if they knew their leader isn’t as strong as they think? Mydei would have lost the respect and loyalty of Kremnoans that he worked tirelessly to gain. The rest of Chrysos Heirs would have regarded him with pity, realizing he doesn’t deserve a seat among them.

Now, though, he is completely alone.

No one to see him crack into pieces or to interrupt him.

Mydei desires nothing more than to rest, to be done with the fucking prophecy. He has given so much of himself already, what else does he have to lose? There is nothing of himself left to offer.

He wishes to slay Nikador but would forego the responsibility to carry the Coreflame of Strife in a heartbeat. He doesn’t want it. Mydei witnessed its corruption firsthand. He refuses to doom the last of Kremnoans like his father had done.

It would be so easy to position the dagger against the wall and push his body against it, to pierce through that one vulnerable spot on his spine and be done with everything for good. But that’s not what he is seeking right now, nor would he ever consciously permanently take his life, he doesn’t think.

Mydei rests his back against a piece of column that failed the trial of time, gazing at the eternal figure of Kephale, bleeding to uphold the burden of life on their shoulders.

He tightens the grip on the dagger and slits his throat in one decisive movement, making sure to sever both of the arteries. He clenches his free hand into a fist to stop the instinct to cover the wound and stall the bleeding, pushing through the dizziness as he waits for the blood loss to take him.

He chokes on ichor as he comes back to life again, smiling at nothing in particular at the image of one of the first Kremnoan feasts hosted in Okhema. He relishes in the joviality of warriors bathing in the glory of a won battle and Krateros toasting to their Prince, gazing down at him like he imagines a proud parent would have. Years before those eyes turned impatient and demanding, refusing to understand Mydei’s motives.

Mydei keeps his eyes closed and takes his life again.

He sees Anaxa, smirking at Mydei from across the room after their short collaboration to get back at Cipher for one of her countless pranks, Aglaea off to his side and pretending she hasn’t the slightest clue what they were up to for once.

Hephaestion’s warm breath against Mydei’s skin, laughing silently as Mydei drank his diluted honey brew, Ptolemy looking up at them with a glare from his beloved book.

Dancing on the battlefield at Phainon’s side, covering each other’s blind spots with ease as they tumbled into a draw of yet another competition.

Golden liquid stains his skin and attire so thoroughly there is barely any other color visible when he opens his eyes by the time he reaches the tenth death. The giant statue of Kephale keeps bleeding alongside him. He stops counting after that.

Mydei is leaning against the wall of one of the houses at the market's entrance, sluggishly trying to recall the schedule he planned out for today a few days prior. The pulsing ache at the center of his forehead proves it difficult to form more complex thoughts. He should have stayed in or holed himself up for another day or two.

“This is new,” Phainon’s voice rings from his side, sending another spike of pain through Mydei as he flinches at the sudden loud sound.

He squints at Phainon, but the man is too preoccupied with staring at Mydei’s neck, one hand already halfway up before Mydei can react. Not that he thinks he would be capable of much at the moment.

His breath doesn’t stutter and his heart doesn’t skip a beat, but Mydei keeps himself as still as he can once Phainon’s fingertips make contact with his throat. They trail along the line, left to right, leaving goosebumps in their wake.

Mydei should have considered the option of breaking into Phainon’s room and stealing one of his chokers to cover the scar up when he woke up in the morning to find it still there. Unfortunately, he was too busy dealing with his head attempting to split itself in half.

“I didn’t hear about you going on a mission,” Phainon continues with a frown, eyes snapping back to meet Mydei’s, thumb still on the carotid artery. “Were you in a fight today?”

Mydei’s body doesn’t retain any scars. There wouldn’t be any healthy tissue left otherwise.

Perhaps it’s his healing factor retaliating against his valiant efforts of forcing himself into the gates of the afterlife. It would be a little foolish to be stuck with that line on his neck for the rest of eternity, though.

Mydei shakes his head minutely, wincing at the way the movement just makes the pain worse. He closes his eyes and tries to breathe through it, clenching his jaw. He would kill himself again if it meant getting over this faster, but since this could be a result of overusing the curse, it might just backfire on him.

His pain tolerance is incredibly high. This headache of his would probably leave an ordinary person dead if it hurts him that much.

“What’s wrong?” Phainon asks with urgency, possibly unused to seeing Mydei out of sorts.

“Migraine,” he whispers, closing his eyes in hopes that taking away one of the senses will calm it down. It’s a lost cause, but he can hope.

“Why are you out here, then?” Phainon questions incredulously, voice pitched lower to accommodate Mydei’s sudden sensitivity.

He grabs Mydei by the forearm and gently steers him away from the market and back in the direction of Marmoreal Palace, presumably with the Chrysos Heirs’ personal quarters in his mind. Mydei sighs and lets himself be led, keeping his eyes shut. He trusts Phainon to keep him safe from tripping or bumping into any citizens loitering around.

Phainon spends the entire day trailing after Mydei hopelessly, even after the migraine subsides enough to be at a manageable level. Mydei is too exhausted to fight him on it, instead choosing to humor him this one time.

It’s— it’s nice. Pleasant. Having Phainon’s attention directed solely at him. Mydei already knew that. He thrives on pushing the other man’s buttons on occasion until Phainon’s vision seems to narrow to him and no one else. But it’s different when Phainon is softer than usual, taking care to relieve Mydei’s pain in any way he can.

Phainon stays by his side all the way until morning comes, inviting himself over to Mydei’s quarters for late dinner and distracting him until he is too sleepy to kick him out properly. When Mydei wakes up a few hours later to the sight of Phainon drooling onto one of Mydei’s pillows, he purposely keeps his mind as blank as possible and gets up to the bathroom.

A flushed image of his face greets him in the mirror, much to his mortification. He splashes some cold water onto the warm skin and inspects himself more thoroughly. The scar on his neck is almost completely gone. He hopes Phainon didn’t inspect it too closely and that he missed the way multiple lines were overlapping over his skin so much it appeared as just one.

Chapter Summary

It happens again. And again, and again. And every time he dies, all he sees is Phainon, Mydei’s brain strangely fixated on him to no end. He notices the tendency for quicker regeneration compared to before as well.

It’s a little overwhelming and quite disconcerting, to put it mildly.

“The human brain is wired in the most intricate of ways,” Anaxa tells him in the Hero’s Bath one day, gesturing with his half-empty goblet.

The only reason he didn’t leave Okhema as soon as his business was done was that Aglaea happened to be otherwise preoccupied for the entire day. It might also have something to do with Hyacine trying her best to convince him he would benefit from even just a few hours of relaxation. He always had a soft spot for her.

Castorice and Hyacine sit not too far away, conversing quietly with one another. Mydei doesn’t entirely understand why he was chosen to be the audience of one when Hyacine is right there until Anaxa continues.

“It’s the last part to die after one’s passing.”

The pieces click together, and Mydei realizes Anaxa is looking for a first-hand recount from him. He could have just asked. Alcohol, even in small quantities, makes him more prone to going off on the tangents.

“Research has been conducted on the significantly injured warriors as well as individuals suffering from sickness who had succumbed to death, and yet healers were successful in the resuscitation.” Mydei resists the urge to yawn, idly wishing Phainon was there to get on Anaxa’s nerves and speed things up. But it’s fine, he will get to the point soon enough. “Vast majority of them expressed being subjected to the sudden visions of their life, witnessing the best of their memories. Supposedly, it is approximated to last a mere few minutes after the person’s death.”

His single eye lands on Mydei, holding his gaze dispassionately, finally done beating around the bush. Mydei raises an eyebrow, waiting for the question.

“So, how does it transpire for you?” Anaxa finally asks. “I imagine you have the most unique understanding of the act of dying itself out of all of us, even Castorice.”

Because Castorice assists with what he cannot do—guiding souls to cross the River of Souls into the afterlife. Her curse places her on par with Death itself, and yet she would still be unable to satisfy Anaxa’s curiosity.

“I always see just one memory,” Mydei explains easily. “The length of it varies. Sometimes, I get a minute before I’m back. Sometimes, it’s hours until I can open my eyes again, usually stuck reliving whatever it is.” Days, if his body faces too heavy of trauma and it happens to align with his psyche taking a toll. “I don’t recall them ever repeating.”

Anaxa nods, brows furrowed in concentration as if he is mentally writing notes on it. “We must take your curse into consideration, of course. The number of memories might be limited due to it, and the time allocated for it could depend on the amount of damage done to your body and its ability to heal it.

“I wonder what would have happened if you were placed in a prolonged coma—would you be stuck in a single memory for days on end even if it's no longer one of the pleasant ones, or would it transform into a different one eventually?” Anaxa mutters under his breath, more to himself than anything else. Mydei doesn’t point out he already knows the answer to being gone for more than one day. His gaze snaps back to focus after a few seconds, regarding Mydei once more. “What of their nature?”

Mydei shrugs, tipping his head up to stare at the high ceiling of the baths. Okheman architecture never disappoints in its details and dimension. The question is simple, he can answer without giving away how they affect him.

“Every moment of my life that has left an impression can make an appearance. I’ve never relieved a memory of training on my own, reading a book, or being idle. Although, I was thrown back to the conversations with people that seem mundane at first glance.”

It could be due to his longevity, leading to running out of sufficient memories considered as above average when most things become shrouded in disinterest with time. Not to mention that he encountered death innumerable times—his brain could be struggling to dig through all the memories to find a new one to display to him. He doesn’t say any of that. It’s Anaxa’s job to draw conclusions.

“Haven’t seen any of my other deaths either despite them having an impact, but there were a few instances where I found myself back at the sea again.”

Anaxa nods in understanding, taking a sip from his drink. There is a moment of silence where Anaxa appears as if he is weighing his words. To say it’s uncharacteristic for him would be an understatement. A feeling of trepidation slinks around at the back of Mydei’s mind.

“Would you say that this phenomenon impacts your psyche, consequently impairing your ability to return, so to say?”

There it is.

It was foolish of Mydei to assume anything would have escaped Anaxa’s attention when it entails a subject he is interested in, whether it focuses on Mydei’s personal life or not. He must have conversed with Castorice on the matter already—she was the one who possibly redirected him to Mydei, expressing her concerns while she was at it.

With a small sigh, Mydei levels him with a flat stare. Anaxa doesn’t cower under it nor does he take the words back.

Mydei’s lack of response is as good as confirmation and they both know it.

“I had to ask,” Anaxa says, quieter than usual. It’s the closest thing to an apology Mydei will ever get.

Mydei doesn’t particularly give a shit, truth be told. He walked into that one, and he knows Anaxa won’t meddle unless it starts impacting the efficiency of his duties.

“I will give you an opportunity to ask one last question,” Mydei decides to change the subject, losing the will to continue with this interrogation. He participated long enough.

“That’s indeed immensely benevolent of you,” Anaxa replies sarcastically but it loses the bite when he takes him up on the offer, nonetheless. He is incredibly easy, at least when it comes to these things. “Does love influence the experience at all?”

Now, Mydei didn’t expect to hear that. It almost pulls a burst of laughter out of him. People always assume he is incapable of such emotion. “Has it escaped your attention that I have never entertained any lovers?” He asks with a wry smile. He fell into bed with a few soldiers from the Kremnoan Detachment in his youth, but that’s not exactly common knowledge in Okhema.

Anaxa seems amused by the reaction. “That’s not the question I asked,” he points out, insufferably, then taps his free hand against the junction of his neck and left shoulder. “You are not an oblivious man, Mydeimos.”

Mydei rolls his eyes, both at the usage of his full name and the not-so-subtle allusion to Phainon. No, Mydei isn’t oblivious to his own feelings for the man, but he isn’t exactly eager to act on them either. Or acknowledge them much, really.

He rises from his seat and stretches briefly, bones popping from sitting in one position for too long. “I’m afraid that doesn't concern you in the slightest, Anaxa.”

Mydei takes pleasure in the way Anaxa’s features twist in a sneer at the nickname he loathes so much. Not that anyone cares about it. To get some more harmless payback, he slips the goblet out of Anaxa’s fingers and downs it in one go, setting it on the table and smirking as Anaxa glares at him with viciousness he could never back up.

Mydei raises an eyebrow in challenge. He wouldn’t mind going against their Scholar, but Phainon would whine about someone stealing his sparring partner once he heard of it.

Anaxa lets out an aggravated breath but otherwise tampers down on the irritation, his gaze once more serious when he regards Mydei. “Would you mind terribly reporting to me if there are any new developments?”

“I cannot begin to guess how many times I have risen from the dead,” Mydei points out slowly. He is as familiar with it as he is with being alive. “The whole process never strayed from its usual course.”

Anaxa waves his fingers at him in clear dismissal, then runs them through his hair, sweeping the fringe back from his eye. “Humor me.”

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

He tears through an enemy’s throat with his gauntlet, turning just in time to see the sharp edge of the blade heading straight at him with inhuman speed. The last thing he sees is the glint of steel in the sun. The last thing he feels is the beginning of a cut on his throat before everything goes blessedly numb as his spine is severed. The last thing that passes through his mind is the realization that he hasn’t ever had his head cut off before.

Does the curse have limitations other than the one spot on his spine? Could it truly be the last time——

Sparks fly as Mydei blocks the sword, skidding back as he digs his heels into the ground. He grins at the thrill that surges through his veins at the sheer power backed behind the blow directed at him. There is nothing quite as riveting as a partner that doesn’t hold back against you, the knowledge of the trust in your ability to match the skill and fight back. The metals make a grinding noise as they unlock their weapons.

Mydei loses track of time as they fight until he sidesteps Phainon and slashes his back with the claws of his gauntlet, sending him stumbling. It could be considered a cheap trick, but they say all is fair in war and love. Their spars could be dragged up to it. Probably. In Mydei’s case, at least. It’s not like Phainon hasn’t done the same before either.

“I just got that coat,” Phainon whines, their spar momentarily forgotten. He tries to crane his head to peek at the damage done to it, spinning in a circle like an idiot when he still cannot catch sight of it.

It pulls a snort out of Mydei against his will. He shouldn’t find something so stupid that funny, but Phainon makes it hard to be truly annoyed at him. Mydei notices the sly grin on his face when he steps closer just a fraction of a second too late. Phainon already throws himself at him with his sword raised between the two of them before he can defend himself adequately.

Mydei has just enough time to angle his arm around Phainon’s body, otherwise staying completely still and letting him push the weapon against his jugular, expression extremely self-satisfied for pulling one over Mydei.

“I won,” Phainon beams, putting the slightest pressure on the blade against Mydei’s skin. It’s not nearly enough to draw blood.

Mydei hums, pressing himself more firmly against it. “Did you?” He smirks back, tracing a sharp metal claw over the ridges of Phainon’s spine through the torn layers of fabric.

Phainon’s back arches at the cold touch, grip on the sword slackening as his body pushes itself against Mydei’s chest with the motion. His eyes widen just a bit in shock, not having expected to have the situation spun around on him. He should have known better by now, after countless instances of fighting with and against Mydei.

“Ah, I hate you,” Phainon mumbles as his head makes a dull thud when he lets it fall on Mydei’s shoulder with resignation. “It’s a draw.”

Mydei lets out a quiet but full-hearted laugh, jostling Phainon as his shoulders shake. His hand settles more firmly on Phainon’s waist to hold him close despite knowing it’s a bad idea to indulge himself like this.

The last thing he notices is the tip of Phainon’s ear, slightly redder than his usual complexion, could it——

Mydei opens his eyes with a sharp intake of breath, head resting on the muddy ground at an awkward angle. It hurts like a bitch, more than any of the resurrections have ever hurt before. Excluding the ones where his body required to be recovered and brought back for observation from the severity of his injuries.

He grits his teeth and picks himself up soundlessly, eyes locked onto the enemies’ backs turned to him. The mindless beasts must have deemed him dead and no longer a thread. Mydei is about to rectify that mistake.

Throughout it, he barely notices the way the corners of his lips are still quirked up, musing at the back of his head that he ought to ask Phainon whether he ever fixed that stupid coat.

Mydei doesn’t reflect much on it. His thoughts briefly jump to the conversation with Anaxa a few months back before disregarding the connection to it.

It’s not even the first time he sees Phainon in his death, after all.

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

The most common cause of Mydei’s deaths is blood loss.

It’s also the least painful one, that drags him under quickly and thoughtlessly. He is so used to it that he can no longer recognize the signs in time, always taken by it at the very last moment. It makes sense, given the way he hasn’t a single care for any wounds sustained in the heat of the battle. Mydei is known to take risks of getting cut and stabbed just to get closer to the enemy to have a clearer shot.

He throws a spear at one of the targets, watching the figure’s body be pinned to the wall behind it. There aren’t any hostiles in close range anymore, so he decides to take a brief moment to catch his breath, heart working overtime to pump his blood at an accelerated speed. And, suddenly, Mydei feels a staggering wave of dizziness hit him.

He curses lowly and tries to keep himself steady as his knees buckle underneath him, already aware of what’s to come.

Black sparks fly through his vision, slowly multiplying. He only catches a glimpse of Phainon turning to check on him from where he is fighting against his own opponent, pushing it off himself roughly as he looks at Mydei in alarm, before everything fades to——

The book falls onto the ground unceremoniously, landing on its open pages with the hardcover up. The title engraved onto it mocks them silently. Mydei looks down blankly, arms crossed. It’s a big volume; the weight of it must have further influenced the impact. There isn't any possibility the paper isn’t creased, if not torn. Heads will roll once Anaxa finds out.

Phainon crouches next to the victim of his carelessness, one hand covering his mouth as he stares at it mournfully. He cautiously reaches out to the book before wincing and retracting his hand, too terrified to check the damage.

“The gravity of the situation might be too much to handle,” Phainon agonizes with the terrible play on words.

Mydei rubs the bridge of his nose in exasperation. He won’t admit he finds it a little humorous, even more so given the fact it’s Phainon who is the culprit. He sure hopes Anaxa won’t consider him an accomplice by association, though.

It’s a very valid concern, actually. And now that he thinks about it, he certainly should make himself scarce as soon as possible before any witnesses stumble upon them. “Right. Best of luck to you.” He turns on his heel to do just that, but unfortunately, he doesn’t get very far.

“Where do you think you’re going?” Phainon asks, clutching onto Mydei’s robe like a child. Mydei whirls around to glare at him, yanking on the material to set it free from its assailant. Phainon only grips it harder and Mydei is forced to let go before it tears. “We are in this together.”

And while, usually, that’s a very correct statement seeing as they somehow end up attached at the hip regardless of what they are doing as of late, Mydei refuses to bear the consequences of this.

“What the fuck do I have to do with this?” Mydei asks, suddenly alarmed. He would fight by Phainon’s side even if the battle was rigged against them in the worst of ways, but dealing with a furious and bitchy Anaxa is not something he will endure willingly.

“You tripped me up,” Phainon accuses, letting go of Mydei to cross his arms with a huff.

“I did no such thing.” Mydei may have tugged on his cape a little. “You stumbled over empty air.”

“Would that empty air be honorable enough to help me, then?” Phainon asks sarcastically, staring at Mydei pointedly.

Mydei wonders when he has become so transparent that he can’t even push Phainon around without being detected. Or perhaps it’s the inability to lie to him convincingly.

Ugh. Fine.

Clicking his tongue in irritation, Mydei crouches alongside him and gathers up the book which Phainon doesn’t feel brave enough to inspect. That’s the perfect Chrysos Heir right there. Titans help them all. Mydei is careful not to add to the damage of it or he truly will become an accomplice. A cursory glance tells him at least five pages are crumpled, and one is nearly torn in half. He looks back to Phainon.

Phainon reads his blank expression accurately, promptly collapsing onto the ground with a loud groan.

“I’m glad to have known you.” Mydei stands back up in one swift move and makes to flee the crime scene, but Phainon’s hand is faster, wrapping around his ankle with too much strength. He tries to shake it off, cursing himself for choosing to wear sandals instead of armor today as it makes it easier for Phainon to keep his iron grip around it.

“You’re not about to abandon your comrade in need, are you?” Phainon asks, aiming for threatening but ending up pathetically resigned. Like Mydei just refused to help him cover up murder instead of intending to leave him alone with a defiled—by Anaxa’s standards—book of all things.

Mydei looks mournfully at the exit one last time before deciding to——

He regains consciousness slowly, as reality comes back to him piece by piece.

His body is carefully arranged on the ground, far from the graceless sprawl he finds himself in whenever he dies on his own. Mydei opens his eyes slowly, blinking a few times to regain his bearings. He looks around, noting the dead bodies littering the ground all around, a half-collapsed wall of a building right behind him.

And Phainon—of course Phainon is there, it’s starting to feel like the man is haunting Mydei—sitting beside him with his knees raised, and one hand propped up on them, his head tilted back to rest against the wall, eyes closed as he controllably breathes in and out. His whole right arm is soaked in blood, and the only reason Mydei doesn’t feel the spike of panic is because it’s the wrong color.

He pushes himself up quietly, swiping his hand through his hair and wincing at the matted feeling of it at the back of his head. He probably hit his head on the way to the ground while dying. He must look like a disaster.

It’s a small mercy that Phainon doesn’t look much better. His hair is stained pink with blood, cuts marring his cheeks and shoulders, having ditched his coat at some point, and a bruise is already forming on his jaw.

He is obviously exhausted and dirty, likely wishing for nothing more than to get back to Okhema so they can clean up and rest. And yet he dragged Mydei all the way to safety and protected his dead body until he woke up. With Mydei’s track record, it could have taken anywhere from a few minutes to actual days. Taking the memory he witnessed into consideration, it couldn’t have been more than an hour. Phainon got lucky.

“You are so stupid,” Mydei still says, thinking back to the damn book that they ended up bribing a Kremnoan specialist to restore it to its original condition before Anaxa could notice.

Phainon jolts, head banging against the wall in shock. “Hello to you too,” he says with a wince, lifting his hand to rub at the spot. “You’ve got an odd way of saying thanks.”

It’s not that Mydei doesn’t appreciate it. He just— Why would anyone bother when he is so used to this?

“You should have dragged me to the camp and let healers handle me,” he says, nudging Phainon’s leg with his foot. “Or better yet, leaving me behind would have been the most optimal course of action.”

Mydei is more than capable of catching up. He would have done another sweep of the area after waking up, ensuring they covered everything. He is quite certain anyone else would have also chosen that route, knowing he would be fine sooner or later.

Phainon gives him a look that says he thinks Mydei is the stupid one out of the two of them which is rich coming from him. “You know me better than that. I’m supposed to watch your back and yet—” He cuts himself off, shaking his head slightly. “It’s the least I could do.”

Mydei resists the urge to roll his eyes, standing up to stretch his muscles. Figures that Phainon would be beating himself up over this. Perfectionist to the core. It doesn’t matter that Mydei hasn’t had to worry about support not even once in all the fights they have gone into together. He cannot say that about anyone else when he cannot bring himself to depend on them to cover for him in a way he trusts Phainon.

“I died because I allowed myself to be stabbed one too many times, Phainon,” he says, bending his neck to the side until it gives a slightly concerning crack. “My back was always secure.”

“I should have noticed,” Phainon argues with a weak glare, brushing his fingers through the blood and dust coating his forehead.

“You should accept you cannot prevent every wrong thing from happening, Deliverer. You are doing more than good enough,” Mydei retorts patiently. He reaches down with his hand to Phainon, waiting until he grasps his fingers around and pulls him up to his feet. “I could not ask for a better partner than you.”

Phainon smiles at him, a small and genuine thing compared to his standard wide grin. He looks pleasantly surprised by Mydei’s admission, squeezing his hand once before letting go.

“Should we check the perimeter for stragglers?”

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

Mydei lurches forward into a sitting position, blood filling his mouth from having bitten on his tongue to instinctively hold back the yell as he had woken up from the nightmare. He runs one hand down his face, inhaling deeply to calm down his racing heartbeat. It doesn’t work quite as well, his breath turning into panting as the image of Leonnius’ body flashes through his mind again, bones protruding from his thighs as he stares through Mydei with vacant eyes.

In the nightmare, he doesn’t express the relief of being able to deliver the news of Mydei’s achievements to the afterlife. Instead, his bloody corpse blames Mydei for the misery brought into the Kremnoans’ lives, cursing him for leading their squad into a trap. Dead eyes bore into him with contempt as Mydei watches the enemy slice through his legs, frozen in place by an invisible force.

The dream makes sense, logically. Mydei always suspected the words were meant just to keep him calm in the retreat. And he never forgave himself for being unable to recover his dear friend’s body. The guilt and grief eat at him during the nights, modifying the memories just to torture him some more for his failure to protect his loved ones. He’s seen that scene play out in five different versions in altering settings, always unable to save his companions despite being right there.

Mydei shakes his head to get rid of any thoughts and gets up. He can’t stay in bed, letting his brain circle through the familiar thought process that will only make him spiral further. His muscles lock in protest as he takes the first step, but he pushes through and stumbles into his private bathroom.

He rests his hands on the sink to support his weight and looks up into the mirror, his breathing pattern still too quick. A sickly pale face greets him, the red of his markings standing out like mortal blood, hair disheveled from the restless sleep, and dark shadows underlining his golden eyes.

So much for the fierce image of the Kremnoan Crown Prince.

His eyes fall to the scissors resting off to the side, usually used to cut through the bandages healers still insist on wrapping around his wounds. On an impulse, he picks them up and takes the few unsteady steps to the shower. He all but collapses in the very corner, pressing his back against the tiled walls as firmly as he can.

He feels like a coward, running from the ghosts of his past. But at the moment, the irrepressible need to witness the moments of his first friends’ happiness and their well-being is stronger than anything else. He has to erase the vision of dead bodies and broken promises, to see the happier memories of what used to be.

Mydei positions the scissors directly above his racing heart and sinks them into his flesh in one firm move, breath escaping him in one short burst as the bone is pierced through and his heart is torn open. He yanks the scissors out to speed up the process, ichor streaming down his body and onto the tile.

It doesn’t take long until his heartbeat stops entirely, and his eyes slip shut on their own accord.

Only to see Phainon instead, some inconsequential memory of walking through the market while they argue over the value of Phainon's latest purchase. It can’t have lasted more than half an hour before he wakes up again. Frustration burns through him, overshadowing the confusion at the realization that he hasn’t seen anything other than Phainon for quite a while now.

He repeats the ordeal, scissors sliding through the ribcage with more ease as the bone is still fragile from the recent recovery, and grits his teeth through the sharp pain.

Phainon, breathless with a laughing fit that overtook him so strongly he cannot even explain what it’s about as Mydei watches on for an unbelievably long time, fighting against the pull on his lips.

Phainon, speaking in quiet tones as he confesses to some of his insecurities, deep into the Curtain-Fall Hour when all of Amphoreus slumbers aside from the two of them, sat side by side with Kephale’s figure as their only witness.

Phainon—

Mydei exhales shakily when he opens his eyes next. It’s frustrating, but it would be bordering on insanity to attempt the exact same thing for the fifth time and expect a different result. Casting away the initial reason for this spiral for the moment, he thinks about the way he was only able to see Phainon out of all possibilities. For a while now, actually.

The thought is concerning.

He reaches up and blindly turns the shower on. He barely feels the freezing water cascading over his head as he watches the gold dilute and swirl down the drain.

At least he doesn’t see Leonnius’ corpse every time he closes his eyes anymore. Now, it’s the last memory of concerned bright blue eyes pushing into his personal space like an annoying pest, his care so obvious even through the sharp jabs at Mydei.

What would Phainon think if he knew Mydei broke apart so easily from one trivial dream?

Would he—

As he cuts the thought off, resolve steels itself somewhere within Mydei’s ribcage where his abused heart thuds in a sluggish beat. He doesn’t want to find out.

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

It happens again. And again, and again. And every time he dies, all he sees is Phainon, Mydei’s brain strangely fixated on him to no end. He notices the tendency for quicker regeneration compared to before as well.

It’s a little overwhelming and quite disconcerting, to put it mildly.

☼ ♆ ☼ ♆ ☼

Mydei comes to quietly, with a breath stuttering into his lungs as if it’s trying to resume the motion that wasn’t performed for a long time. His mind is shrouded in a fog, throat impossibly dry and limbs stiff.

There is a vague memory still clinging to the forefront of his brain, of bright hair and eyes, days filled with easy companionship. He frowns, trying to catch it before it can slip away from him. Was he dreaming about it? It seems unlikely. His nights are barely ever spent reliving the pleasant memories.

No, he only sees those under one circumstance.

Does it mean he died again?

Why doesn’t he remember it, then?

He tries to move but his body feels too heavy, managing only a small spasm in his legs. There weren’t many instances where he had been incapacitated to this extent, he must have encountered something particularly powerful if he was left in such a state. Could it be black tide?

With great effort he manages to blink his eyes open, squinting against the blurry vision. The first thing he recognizes is that he is at the healer’s, the décor of the room as familiar to him as his own quarters. The light is dimmed, curtains drawn to shield him from the intense sunlight that would have shined directly onto his bed otherwise. He appreciates the effort.

When he manages to shift his head just slightly, he notices the even more familiar figure of a man slumped onto his bed, head propped up on the forearms and light hair strewn on the mattress as soft snores echo in the quiet room.

Mydei winces, eyes slipping shut when pain attempts to split his head open again. Some memories come back to him. A few scenes of walking side by side, pushing each other, and bickering over the smallest of things out of boredom resurface in quick succession. Walking into an unknown city together and observing as Phainon tries his best to haggle over an antique of sorts. Those evidently don’t portray what happened before Mydei must have died as his brain sluggishly supplies that it’s from an expedition that took place two years ago. Aglaea forced them into taking it when they were acting out a little too much in Okhema from restlessness, making use of their overflowing energy to help a settlement falling to the black tide.

The few moments that just flashed through his mind he can recall stretching over the days. Is it his brain supplying more than he might have initially seen after death, or did it really take that long to come back?

Question after question buzzes in his brain even though his body feels heavier than when he first woke up. With some struggle, he opens his eyes again and immediately zeroes in on Phainon. He is dressed in loose-fitting clothes for once, but his back is bent at a strange angle like he didn’t intend to fall asleep at all when fatigue took over. There are almost-healed cuts littering the slivers of skin that Mydei can glimpse, hair unwashed and fingers fisted into the bedsheet with desperation.

Mydei wants to wake him up because that position cannot be comfortable and Phainon will be whining about the backache for days to come. His voice fails him, lips barely moving when he tries to command them to speak. There is no hope to shift his hand over and grab Phainon’s, or even to tug on his hair. Two of his fingers twitch but that’s the best he can do, frozen in his own body.

He blinks a few times when his eyes threaten to close without permission, his head swimming in the onslaught of dizziness. It’s already a lost battle before he can even think about it, overtaken with sleep as suddenly as he had woken up.

chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

There is pity in the way Anaxa regards him. “Most people would be making use of what little time we have, then.”

“It would be cruel, considering that we know not how or when we will meet our demise, a permanent one in my case. Why give life to something that can only end in agony?”

“Why are they so mean to me?” Phainon asks resignedly, jerking his arm up and down. The chimera dangles in the air along with it, its teeth embedded in Phainon’s sleeve with vicious tenacity.

It’s been hours since they were first roped into supervising six young chimeras. Mydei wasn’t listening when they were told why the animals couldn’t be roaming free just yet. He and Phainon were left to their devices in the corner of the Garden of Life, citizens occasionally coming by to fawn over the adorable creatures. They might be ogling Phainon just a bit while they’re at it, but one impatient glare from Mydei manages to do a good job of sending them away.

“They sense you’re not so saintly as you like everyone to believe,” Mydei says over the loud purring of four chimeras curled up on top of each other in his lap.

Mydei has a sneaking suspicion that Aglaea orchestrated this to force them into getting rest. He might be inclined to admit that they’ve been overdoing it with their expeditions out of Okhema to help the settlements filled with too many people to be allowed past the gates to the Eternal Holy City.

“That’s just rude. I am a good person,” Phainon protests half-heartedly, but his shoulders shrink down on himself in dejection just a bit. It appears to be one of the days where he doesn't take the snarky comments well. Mydei doubts anyone else would even notice.

“You are the best of us,” Mydei replies without missing a beat, with as much conviction as he can put into it so that Phainon doesn’t get any ideas about it being untrue. “But you are also a menace when you want to be.”

Phainon chuckles at that, tension easing. He pulls his arm closer to himself, trying to pry the chimera’s jaw open with a finger to get it to release him without being too forceful. It growls at him, the sound muffled in the fabric. Phainon sighs and looks at Mydei helplessly.

Alright, it might be time to rescue him.

Mydei leans over, careful to not jostle the animals resting in his lap, and gently picks up the unruly chimera by the middle with one hand, reaching around with his other to rub against its snout and allow it to scent him. It lets go without much fuss, tilting its head to lick his fingers.

“Of course they love you,” Phainon mutters under his breath, but there is nothing but fondness sparkling in his eyes.

“It’s because you are too restless,” Mydei explains with a hum. Phainon is generally a ball of energy and anxiety in equal measure, and the chimeras react to it in a stand-offish manner.

On an impulse, he grabs Phainon’s hand and presses their palms together, then brings them close to the chimera very slowly. It lets out a small awoo before nudging against their hands, nuzzling its head against Phainon’s. Phainon’s fingers twitch like he wants to scratch its fur, but Mydei tightens his hold, Phainon’s hand relaxing immediately. He then moves their hands together, petting along the chimera’s fur gently until it warms up to the touch before retracting his hand entirely and letting Phainon do his thing.

The chimera doesn’t notice the change, purring as Phainon continues on. Phainon’s jaw is slacked open, as his eyes shift rapidly from the animal to Mydei, like he’s asking whether Mydei is also seeing what is happening.

Mydei chuckles at it, watching as Phainon smiles at him as if he had hung all the stars, eyes sparkling with——

Mydei jolts awake, muscles spasming as he regains the feeling and control over them all at once. He feels lost for all of a second before his surroundings make sense and his brain realizes he’s been through another death. Right.

“Glad to see you back among the living,” Phainon says through a yawn, clearly having spent the night in the uncomfortable chair in the infirmary by Mydei’s side. Like he often does.

Mydei’s head hurts. Just the regular kind of pain, easily managed by ignoring it until it goes away. But what makes it worse, is the confusion at his predicament. The memories returning to him in death used to vary in time and people who appeared in them. Why is it always Phainon nowadays?

“Fuck you,” Mydei says, hoarsely. He feels like he is losing his mind.

Phainon’s mouth locks mid-yawn and he blinks down at him stupidly, tilting his head with confusion. It’s probably fair, he hasn’t even done anything to earn Mydei’s ire as of late.

“What have I done this time?” Phainon asks tiredly, except it’s filled with affection as he passes Mydei a glass of water without missing a beat.

Mydei huffs and takes a few careful sips of the drink, watching as some of the strain disappears from Phainon’s shoulders as he leans back onto the chair, hair falling into his eyes.

“Exist,” Mydei says flatly. He is confident half of his problems wouldn’t have ever occurred if not for Phainon, be it bringing him headache after headache, annoying him into eventually doing whatever Phainon wants, or being a menace in general.

But, Okhema wouldn’t feel as much of a… home as it does, if Phainon didn’t make it so.

The way they naturally gravitate toward one another, always aware of where to find the other without asking. Seeing through the cracks of the carefully crafted masks, understanding the insecurities and worries without the need to express them aloud.

“Sorry, I guess.” Phainon snorts quietly, swiping his hair back from his face. He smiles sleepily at Mydei but makes no move to head to his own bed now that he has witnessed him regain his full health. “You will have to endure my presence until Titans themselves force me away.”

Mydei closes his eyes briefly, inhaling deeply and holding it in his lungs.

He knows that devotion runs deep through Phainon’s veins, mirrored by Mydei’s own conviction. They are so intertwined—have been for a while now, really—that perhaps it is a natural trajectory for his brain to be wrapped around Phainon’s very existence so tightly.

It doesn’t mean it isn’t annoying and frustrating to the bone, and that there isn’t fear lurking around. That one day he will forget the faces of his closest friends without the option to relive the more carefree days he spent with them. But it might be too late to prevent this change.

i don't know what happened, this was supposed to be 14k words in total. i guess you can treat a doubled word count as an apology for taking this long?
also this isn't 100% edited because it's late and i don't know what i'm reading anymore

small explanation because i think it's obvious but i'm also tweaking thinking it might not be: mydei's regen went down after he got to okhema and allowed himself to sort through what he went through, trauma response, depression, etc. then it gradually goes back to its original state as he heals, whether he realizes or not, by having steady support in phainon, experiencing so much love directed at him, and having someone he cares about so deeply as well. so, by the time we hit canon it's back to it's perfect state
that's not to say his mental health is squeaky lol. he and phainon are lowkey codependent, their lives revolving around one another. also look at the last few sentences — mydei has learned nothing, he still reverts to "if things are bad, i can always fall back on the memories", he simply changed his anchor (so he is more stable, yes)

i also hope that the transition between a memory and life isn't too confusing. i wanted it to be a very quick transition, something disorienting which mydei loses himself in, because it feels like he is experiencing it all over again and he himself isn't aware he is dead during it. in the end, i went back and added an additional "—" to every transition cuz i overuse that shit outside of it too

you can tell when i started to think "damn. i should learn to pace better and write longer scenes" lmfao. that being said, it's actually a goal of mine. if i manage to get out another work for phaidei, it's going to be much longer. more thorough characterization, hopefully more world-building, phainon pov instead of mydei for once, more npcs, and most of all better pacing and longer scenes, like i said. i'm not making any promises, my track record is horrendous. i would love nothing more than to write it, truly. but it's not exactly up to me seeing as my interest in ships fades fast. i'm not over phaidei just yet, but this was difficult to finish. since i'm done, i have to take care of two pretty time consuming tasks i was prioritizing writing over. i'm not sure i will have motivation to write afterwards lmao. that being said, i could very well come back in three months with some 80k word giant, you never know with me (hell, i never thought i would write four whole works for any ship)
